title: Deprecation Strategy
description: Build a complete API deprecation workflow using headers, monitoring, client notifications, and automated enforcement.

data.text: Deprecation is the process of retiring an old API version while giving clients time to migrate. Without a formal deprecation strategy, old versions accumulate indefinitely. With one, you can clean up technical debt on a predictable schedule.

items: Announce — publish deprecation notice with sunset date and migration guide
Warn — return Deprecation and Sunset headers on old endpoints
Monitor — track v1 traffic; identify slow adopters
Enforce — return 410 Gone after sunset date
Remove — delete old code and infrastructure

rows: Date when the endpoint will be removed

data.text: Example: Deprecation Filter in ASP.NET Core

data.title: Global deprecation filter returning Sunset headers
data.content: Apply a result filter to all v1 endpoints to signal deprecation and guide clients to v2.

data.text: Track which clients are still using deprecated versions. Use the User-Agent header, API keys, or a custom X-Client-ID header to identify integrations.

items: List all clients making >100 requests/day to deprecated endpoints
Send email notifications at 12 months, 6 months, 3 months, and 1 month before sunset
Provide a migration guide with code examples for each client SDK
Offer extended support contracts for enterprise clients who cannot migrate on time

data.title: Deprecation without a date is just nostalgia
data.text: Publishing deprecation warnings without a sunset date has no effect. Clients will ignore the warning indefinitely. Always pair Deprecation: true with a specific Sunset date.

data.title: Post-sunset response for v1 clients
data.content: After the sunset date, old endpoints return 410 Gone with a structured error body.
data.code:
HTTP/1.1 410 Gone
Deprecation: true
Sunset: Sat, 31 Oct 2026 23:59:59 GMT
Link: </v2/users>; rel="successor-version"
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "error": {
    "code": "DeprecatedVersionGone",
    "message": "v1 was sunset on 2026-10-31.",
    "sunsetDate": "2026-10-31T23:59:59Z",
    "successorVersion": "v2",
    "migrationGuide": "/docs/migration/v1-to-v2"
  }
}

items.question: How long should a deprecation period last?
items.answer: 12 months is standard for public APIs. For internal APIs with controlled clients, 3-6 months is sufficient. Enterprise contracts may require 18-24 months.

items.question: Can I restart the deprecation clock?
items.answer: Avoid restarting. It erodes trust. If you must extend, communicate the reason clearly and provide a firm new sunset date. Repeated extensions signal poor planning.

items.question: What if a client keeps calling v1 after sunset?
items.answer: Return 410 Gone with a structured error. If the client has a paid support contract, offer a grace period. Do not silently keep v1 running; it creates security and maintenance debt.

data.title: Key takeaway
points: Deprecation is a contract, not a suggestion.
Pair Deprecation: true with a firm Sunset date.
Track client migration progress and notify slow adopters.
410 Gone is the professional way to end a version.
data.takeaway: A deprecation strategy is how you pay down technical debt without surprising your users. Announce early, warn loudly, and enforce on schedule.
